newsitem.title: UK: Minor metals quiet, Russian stockpiles overshadowed.
newsitem.headline: Minor metals quiet, Russian stockpiles overshadowed.

text.p: Trading in industrial minor metals was mostly at a low ebb this week, but some showed signs of cracking under downside pressure against a backdrop of trader talk about off loading of Russian stockpiled material.
Several said they were sure that Russian reserves had started to enter the market.

Recently traders said they believed that 420 tonnes of cobalt, 30,000 76-lb flasks of mercury, 7,000 tonnes of titanium sponge and an undisclosed amount of chrome could be released from strategic stockpiles.
"The group of metals named in the Russian stockpile have started to ease or are looking toppy," one trader commented.
On cobalt, one trader said that most of the metal had entered the market but believed that it had found buyers from consumers to cover their commitments.
Cobalt has the potential to withstand new supply but one trader suggested that further sales from Russia will be seen near-term.
"There are additional amounts of Russian cobalt in the pipeline," one European trader said. "Negotiations are in place from Russian reserves."
Russian authorities would not comment on the talk.
Despite the plight of war-ravaged Zaire, a producer of cobalt, prices eased. Cobalt is often pressured lower by traders around the time of US DLA sales.
On Wednesday the Defence National Stockpile Centre said it released invitations for bids for approximately 1 million pounds of cobalt under the sealed bid format.
A second offering under the invitation is planned for May 1997.
Russian cobalt was trading in a range of between $18 and $19 a lb according to some traders.
Others said their range was lower at roughly between $17 and $18. In mid-January prices commanded levels of around $20.
Despite the drift most of the traders polled by Reuters believed prices had the potential to snap higher.
"It may have to drift towards $15/$16 before a recovery emerges...consumers are likely to cover at these lower levels" one trader said.
High grade material was around $20/$21, against $22/$23 in late January.
Indium continued to firm against the backdrop of brisk Japanese demand. Traders said that Chinese producers were still extremely oversold.
Several traders said prices could climb further over the coming weeks towards $300.
They noted that major producer Indium Corp of America has raised its indium price by $15 to $225 per kg or $7 per troy ounce effective Feb 26.
For around 15 months Indium Corp has consistently lowered prices. Traders saw the hike in the price as a signal to further gains.
Oversupplied rhodium continued to ease, with several traders forecasting further declines near-term.
Investment fund selling was also noted in rhodium.
Magnesium was in over supply.

Traders noted news that magnesium inventories continue to rise. The International Magnesium Association said that global inventories at the end of 1996 totalled 42,100 tonnes, up 19,300 tonnes from the end of 1995.
Vanadium after recent solid gains eased back under profit-taking. Antimony remained in the doldrums as major players remained sidelined. But several traders suggested activity was soon to pick up.
Elsewhere the other minor metals remained quiet at little changed levels.
